title: Jesuit Reducciones
capsule: The Jesuit Reducciones were a network of mission townships established by the Society of Jesus from 1609 among the Guaraní-speaking peoples of the Río de la Plata basin, spanning territory in present-day Paraguay, Argentina, and Brazil. At peak extent in the early 18th century the system comprised some thirty missions housing over 100,000 Guaraní in communities that combined Catholic liturgy with indigenous communal agriculture, craft production, and a notable degree of Guaraní self-governance. The Guaraní militias organized under Jesuit direction successfully repelled Portuguese Bandeirante slave-raiding expeditions on several occasions. When the Society of Jesus was expelled from Spanish America by royal decree in 1767, the mission system collapsed within a generation; the surviving communities dispersed or were absorbed into colonial towns.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The locations of individual mission towns are archaeologically known, but the aggregate polygon representing mission territorial influence is only approximately bounded, as the Guaraní-controlled hinterland had no formal frontier demarcation.
